nameStory: The 'oblique' in this beetle's name refers to the slanted or diagonal patterns often found on the polypore fungi where it makes its home. 'Polypore' describes the bracket fungi with tiny pores on their undersides, which this beetle calls both dinner table and nursery. It's like having an apartment that's also your favorite restaurant!
description: The Oblique Polypore Fungus Beetle is a small, dark beetle that specializes in living on and eating bracket fungi growing on trees. These beetles are primarily black or dark brown with a distinctive bright orange shield-shaped patch (called a scutellum) right behind their head. They're typically about 1/4 to 1/2 inch long and have a somewhat flattened, oval body shape perfect for crawling into the crevices of their fungal homes.

idTips.label: Bright Orange Shield
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable bright orange triangular patch right behind the beetle's head - it glows like a tiny traffic cone against the dark body and is visible even from several feet away

idTips.label: Dark Body Color
idTips.description: The rest of the beetle is deep black to dark reddish-brown with a slightly glossy sheen that catches light when the beetle moves

idTips.label: Flattened Body Shape
idTips.description: The beetle feels firm but somewhat flattened when gently handled, allowing it to squeeze into tight spaces between fungal layers

idTips.label: Fungal Habitat
idTips.description: Always found on or very near polypore bracket fungi - look for the white, brown, or shelf-like fungi growing from tree trunks and fallen logs

idTips.label: Slow Movement
idTips.description: Moves deliberately and somewhat sluggishly compared to other beetles, often remaining motionless when first disturbed

habitat: Look for these beetles on polypore bracket fungi growing from dead or dying hardwood trees, particularly oak, maple, and birch throughout New England's forests. They prefer the larger, well-established shelf fungi on standing dead trees or recently fallen logs in moist woodland areas. You'll find them from sea level to mid-elevations, wherever their fungal hosts are thriving in shaded forest environments.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots to mate and lay eggs in fresh fungal growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen crawling on bracket fungi, feeding and reproducing in the warm, humid conditions.
seasonality.fall: Still active through early fall, with late-season adults preparing for winter by burrowing deeper into their fungal homes.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden deep within bracket fungi or under loose bark, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: These beetles are essentially living recycling machines - they help break down dead wood by eating the fungi that are already decomposing the tree, creating a three-way partnership between beetle, fungus, and dead wood that speeds up forest renewal by decades!
confusionNotes: The only other Penthe beetle in North America is Penthe pimelia, but it lacks the bright orange shield completely - if you see that glowing orange patch, you've definitely found the oblique species. Memory trick: 'Orange Oblique' - both words start with vowels and this is the one with the bright beacon!
contextualKnowledge: The term 'scutellum' for that orange shield comes from Latin meaning 'little shield' - it's the same word used for the shields carried by Roman soldiers. Entomologists use this term for the triangular plate found behind the head in many beetles and other insects.
compareHints: Since this is the only Penthe species you'll encounter in New England, compare it with other small dark beetles found on fungi. Most other fungus-dwelling beetles lack the distinctive bright orange scutellum entirely. The orange shield is so unique among New England's beetle fauna that it makes this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.
